domain_label: Study System — Visual-Encoding & Graph-View Cartographer: Semantic Zoom, Level-of-Detail & Graph Drawing
purpose: How the concept knowledge graph is DRAWN as an interactive semantic-zoom map: the cartographic-generalization science that decides what to show, hide, aggregate and rename at each zoom level (few category headings zoomed out, concise concept names as you zoom in), plus the graph-drawing machinery — force-directed and hierarchical layout, edge bundling, and label decluttering — that turns the Concept/ConceptEdge data into a legible, honest, performant picture, kept truthful by tagging every domain-science claim ESTIMATE-to-source-verify and every app fact to APP_RECON.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors and every layout/LOD choice is an ESTIMATE synthesized from information-visualization and cartography domain knowledge, not measured on this app's graph

the app has Concept and ConceptEdge entities (prereq/related/part_of edge types) but NO installed graph library and NO page that renders any graph, so this KB specifies a drawn view that does not yet exist [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.5]

domain-science references (semantic-zoom/ZUI lineage, cartographic generalization operators, force-directed and layered layout, edge bundling, NP-hard label placement) are stated from confident general knowledge but were NOT source-verified in this session, so they are carried as [ESTIMATE — to source-verify] rather than cited to a specific title/year

the MEANING encoded by color (high-yield intensity, mastery green/gray/red-dot) and the analytics charts beyond the day-box are neighboring KBs in this same specialist; this KB owns only geometry, zoom, generalization and layout
exclusions: the color system that encodes meaning (brightness-coded high-yield intensity, mastery-state green/gray/red-dot, colorblind-safe perceptual palettes) — neighboring viz KB — beyond consuming a node's precomputed importance/mastery as a selection and label input
the analytics charts (calibration trends, mastery-over-time) beyond the day-box — neighboring viz KB — since those are statistical-chart encodings, not graph drawing

the knowledge-graph DATA and meaning layer (node/edge schema, hub/prerequisite structure, terminology linking) owned by the kgraph specialist — this KB draws whatever graph kgraph defines and does not decide its ontology

the actual pixel styling and component code, exact library API calls, and any invented graph-library benchmark numbers — the KB specifies decision criteria, not an implementation or fabricated performance figures

glossary.definition: Zoom that changes WHAT is represented and HOW at each scale — a coarse level shows category headings, a fine level shows individual concepts with fuller names — as opposed to geometric zoom, which only scales the same fixed picture; the mechanism behind 'few nodes zoomed out, more detail and concise names zoomed in' [ESTIMATE — zoomable-user-interface lineage, to source-verify].

A ladder of discrete zoom levels, each with a target visual-complexity budget (how many nodes, edges and labels may appear), that the generalization operators are applied to satisfy; borrowed from computer-graphics LOD and cartographic scale bands [ESTIMATE — to source-verify].

The map-making science of representing less detail at smaller scale through operators — selection/elimination, simplification, aggregation, typification, displacement, symbolization — repurposed here to decide which concept nodes, edges and labels appear at each zoom level [ESTIMATE — operator taxonomy, to source-verify].

Collapsing a cluster of concepts (e.g. an INBDE FK area or CC section) into a single super-node heading at coarse zoom that expands into its member concepts as the user zooms in, with a fixed, honest membership mapping.

A physics-analogy layout in which edges act as springs pulling connected nodes together while all node pairs repel, iterated until the energy/stress is minimized, yielding an organic clustering; scales from O(n^2) to O(n log n) with a Barnes-Hut quadtree approximation [ESTIMATE — spring-embedder/stress methods, to source-verify].

A layout for directed acyclic graphs that assigns nodes to layers, minimizes edge crossings between adjacent layers, then assigns coordinates, making prerequisite flow read top-to-bottom; requires cycles to be broken first for layout purposes [ESTIMATE — layered/Sugiyama-style, to source-verify].

Routing near-parallel or hierarchically related edges along shared paths so a dense graph shows its overall flow instead of a hairball, trading away the traceability of any single edge [ESTIMATE — hierarchical/force-directed bundling, to source-verify].

Placing node labels without overlap by collision detection, priority ordering and zoom thresholds (only important/visible nodes are labelled at coarse zoom); the underlying point-feature label-placement problem is NP-hard and solved greedily/heuristically [ESTIMATE — to source-verify].

Keeping node positions stable across zoom levels, expansions and re-layouts (incremental layout, pinned anchors, animated transitions) so the user does not lose track of where things are when the view changes.

The rule that a zoomed-out summary must faithfully represent what it hides — no invented groupings, member counts and coverage visible, mastery/high-yield roll-ups computed as real aggregates — so removing detail never implies a structure that is not in the data.

The drawn view is a cartography problem (what to show at each scale) fused with a graph-drawing problem (where to put nodes and edges), kept honest and legible.

nodes.definition: Fix the core distinction that drives everything downstream. GEOMETRIC zoom scales one fixed picture: zooming in makes the same nodes and labels larger, zooming out makes them smaller until unreadable. SEMANTIC zoom changes WHAT is drawn and its representation at each level: a coarse level shows a handful of category headings, a fine level shows individual concepts with their own names and edges — new objects appear and old ones change form, not just size [ESTIMATE — zoomable-user-interface lineage, to source-verify]. The requirement 'few nodes/headings zoomed out, more detail and more concise-then-fuller names as you zoom in' is by definition a semantic-zoom requirement; geometric zoom alone cannot satisfy it because it cannot add or rename objects.

nodes.definition: Structure semantic zoom as a level-of-detail hierarchy: a small ladder of discrete zoom levels, each with an explicit visual-complexity BUDGET — a target ceiling on how many nodes, edges and labels may appear on screen so the view stays legible rather than a hairball [ESTIMATE — LOD from graphics and cartographic scale bands, to source-verify]. Each level's budget is what the generalization operators are applied to satisfy: the coarsest level might allow only a dozen heading meta-nodes, the finest a few hundred concept nodes within the viewport. Discrete levels (with hysteresis at the thresholds to avoid flicker) are chosen over continuous morphing because they make per-level authoring, labelling and testing tractable.

nodes.definition: Adopt the cartographic generalization operators as the vocabulary for meeting each LOD budget [ESTIMATE — operator taxonomy from map generalization, to source-verify]: SELECTION/ELIMINATION (drop or keep whole features), SIMPLIFICATION (reduce a feature's detail), AGGREGATION (merge many features into one), TYPIFICATION (replace a dense group by a representative few that preserve its pattern), DISPLACEMENT (nudge features apart so they remain distinct), and SYMBOLIZATION (change how a feature is drawn, e.g. a cluster becomes a heading glyph). Mapped to the graph: eliminate low-importance nodes at coarse zoom, aggregate clusters into meta-nodes, typify a hub's many leaves by a labelled count, displace overlapping nodes, and symbolize a collapsed region as a single heading. These operators are the concrete moves generalization makes; they are not app-specific and are borrowed wholesale from map-making.

their mapping onto graph nodes, edges and labels
excluded: the importance ranking that drives selection (its own node)
the meta-node membership mapping (its own node)

pros.claim: A named operator set makes generalization a checklist of concrete moves rather than ad-hoc hiding
pros.example: choosing typification (a labelled '+40 more') over blunt elimination when a hub has many leaf concepts

cons.claim: The operators are a cartographic import whose exact taxonomy this KB did not source-verify, so names/counts may differ from the canonical reference
cons.example: treating typification and aggregation as cleanly separate when a specific source may split them differently

failure_modes: hiding detail with no operator discipline so the overview is arbitrary
applying displacement so aggressively that positions no longer reflect structure
acceptance_tests: the node enumerates selection/aggregation/simplification/typification/displacement/symbolization, maps them onto graph elements, and tags the taxonomy ESTIMATE-to-source-verify

nodes.definition: Specify how the selection/elimination operator decides which nodes survive at coarse zoom: an IMPORTANCE RANKING orders every node, and only the top-ranked survive to the coarsest levels while the rest are eliminated or absorbed into an aggregate. Importance blends structural centrality (hub degree / prerequisite fan-out in the ConceptEdge graph), high-yield weight, and mastery relevance (a confidently weak concept the learner needs is worth keeping visible) [ESTIMATE — design synthesis over standard graph-centrality and the app's own importance signals]. A pure degree cut is rejected because it would drop a low-degree but high-yield or weak concept the user most needs; importance must be a deliberate blend so the overview surfaces what matters, not merely what is well-connected.

top-ranked nodes surviving to coarse levels

excluded: the color encoding of high-yield/mastery (neighboring KB)

nodes.definition: Define aggregation: collapse a cluster of related concepts into a single META-NODE (a heading) at coarse zoom that expands into its member concepts as the user zooms in. The natural clusters for this app are the INBDE taxonomy groupings the pipeline already uses — FK areas and CC sections (mastery is already averaged per 'fk|N' and 'cc|DTP/OHM/PP') — so an FK area becomes one heading node zoomed out and its concepts appear zoomed in [FACT-source: APP_RECON — pipeline averages mastery per FK area and CC section]. The membership mapping (which concept belongs to which meta-node) must be FIXED and honest, not recomputed differently per frame, so a heading always contains the same members. Aggregation is what makes the coarse level a 'few headings' view and gives the expand/collapse interaction its structure.

nodes.definition: Realize the 'concise names zoomed out, fuller names zoomed in' requirement as label generalization: each drawable element carries per-LOD-level label VARIANTS. At the coarsest level a meta-node shows a short category heading (e.g. 'Pharmacology'); at mid zoom a concept shows a concise name; at the finest zoom it shows its fuller, disambiguated name. Labels are authored or derived per level and keyed to the ZOOM_LOD_MAPPING, never by naive string truncation that could mangle a term [ESTIMATE — design synthesis; abbreviation must preserve meaning]. This is the label side of semantic zoom: as the user zooms in, both MORE labels appear (more nodes are labelled) and each label grows from a terse form toward its full concept name.

nodes.definition: Enforce the honesty contract on abstraction: a zoomed-out summary must faithfully represent what it hides. Concretely — a meta-node heading must group ONLY its real members (no invented or vanity groupings), it should expose member COUNT and coverage so the user knows how much is folded inside, and any rolled-up value (a heading's mastery or high-yield intensity) must be a REAL aggregate of its members, not a hand-picked or cosmetic number [ESTIMATE — design synthesis binding this KB to the factory honesty contract]. Hiding detail for legibility is legitimate; implying a structure, completeness or mastery that the data does not support is not. This is the visualization analogue of the KB honesty tags: the overview may say less, but everything it says must be true.

showing member counts/coverage
roll-ups as real aggregates not cosmetic numbers
excluded: the exact color mapping of a rolled-up value (neighboring KB)

nodes.definition: Specify force-directed layout as the default for the general (related-edge) graph: model edges as springs pulling connected nodes together and all node pairs as mutually repelling charges, then iterate until the total energy/stress is minimized, producing an organic layout where tightly linked concepts cluster and unrelated ones spread apart [ESTIMATE — spring-embedder and stress-majorization methods, to source-verify]. It needs no predefined hierarchy, adapts to arbitrary edge structure, and reveals community structure visually, which suits the 'related' ConceptEdge type. Its costs — a naive O(n^2) repulsion step, non-determinism, and instability under change — are addressed by the scaling and stability nodes that follow.

included: spring attraction plus pairwise repulsion minimizing energy/stress
organic clustering suited to related edges
naming its cost/instability handed to later nodes
excluded: the Barnes-Hut scaling approximation (next node)
the layered layout for directed prereq edges (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a non-determinism complaint or a scale threshold crossing changes the layout choice

pros.claim: Force-directed layout needs no predefined structure and visually clusters related concepts, matching the related-edge graph
pros.example: concepts that share many 'related' edges settling into a visible community without any manual grouping

cons.claim: It is non-deterministic, unstable under edits, and naively O(n^2), so large or changing graphs need extra machinery
cons.example: the same graph laid out twice giving mirrored or rotated results that disorient a returning user

failure_modes: running naive O(n^2) repulsion on a large graph and freezing the browser
letting non-determinism reposition everything on each load
acceptance_tests: the node defines spring attraction plus pairwise repulsion minimizing energy/stress, ties it to the related-edge graph, and names its O(n^2)/instability costs deferred to later nodes, tagged ESTIMATE-to-source-verify
revisit_triggers: layout non-determinism disorients users
the graph grows past the naive-cost threshold
a stress-majorization variant is adopted

nodes.definition: Address force-directed layout's scaling: the pairwise repulsion is O(n^2) per iteration, which does not survive a graph of hundreds-to-thousands of concepts. The standard remedy is a Barnes-Hut quadtree approximation that groups distant nodes into cells and approximates their combined repulsion, reducing each iteration to about O(n log n) [ESTIMATE — Barnes-Hut n-body approximation applied to graph layout, to source-verify]. Combined with a capped iteration count and a cooling schedule, this keeps layout interactive at the app's planned scale (the owner plans 2000+ cards, and the pipeline already imposes 500-row query caps that this view must respect) [FACT-source: APP_RECON — 2000-card plan and 500-row caps]. Scaling is a precondition for choosing a render target and for viewport culling.

included: the O(n^2)-to-O(n log n) Barnes-Hut approximation
capped iterations and cooling for interactivity
respecting the app's scale and 500-row caps
excluded: the render-target (SVG/canvas) choice (its own node)
viewport culling (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a persistent stall or a cap-forced paging changes the scaling approach

pros.claim: Barnes-Hut brings force-directed cost down to roughly O(n log n), making layout feasible at the app's 2000+ node scale
pros.example: laying out a two-thousand-concept graph in bounded iterations instead of a quadratic blow-up

cons.claim: The approximation trades exactness for speed and adds a quadtree parameter (opening angle) that mis-set can distort layout
cons.example: too coarse an opening angle merging distinct clusters' repulsion and blurring their separation

failure_modes: shipping naive O(n^2) and freezing at scale
mis-tuning the quadtree approximation so clusters distort
acceptance_tests: the node gives the O(n^2)-to-O(n log n) Barnes-Hut approximation with capped iterations/cooling, and ties feasibility to the app's 2000+ scale and 500-row caps (APP_RECON), tagged ESTIMATE-to-source-verify
revisit_triggers: layout still stalls at scale
the quadtree opening angle distorts clusters
the 500-row cap forces paged loading

nodes.definition: Specify hierarchical (layered) layout for the DIRECTED prerequisite structure: the ConceptEdge 'prereq' edges form a directed graph whose flow (what must be learned before what) reads best as layers. A layered layout assigns each node to a layer consistent with edge direction, minimizes edge crossings between adjacent layers, then assigns coordinates so the prerequisite flow runs cleanly in one direction [ESTIMATE — layered/Sugiyama-style layout, to source-verify]. It requires the prereq subgraph to be acyclic; any cycle must be detected and an edge temporarily reversed for layout purposes only. Force-directed layout suits the 'related' edges while layered layout suits the 'prereq' edges, so the view uses each where it fits rather than forcing one algorithm on both edge types.

included: layer assignment, crossing minimization, coordinate assignment for prereq edges
the DAG requirement and cycle-breaking for layout
using layered for prereq and force-directed for related edges
excluded: the force-directed layout itself (prior node)
edge bundling of the layered edges (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a prereq cycle or a confusing hybrid changes the layered-layout use

pros.claim: Layered layout makes prerequisite flow read directionally, which force-directed layout cannot show
pros.example: foundational concepts sitting in top layers and dependent ones below so the learning order is visible

cons.claim: It demands an acyclic prereq graph and can sprawl wide, and mixing it with force-directed layout complicates the combined view
cons.example: a prereq cycle in the data breaking layer assignment until an edge is reversed for layout

failure_modes: running layered layout on a cyclic prereq graph and getting a broken assignment
forcing one layout on both edge types and losing either flow or clustering
acceptance_tests: the node describes layer assignment, crossing minimization and coordinate assignment for prereq edges, requires a DAG with cycle-breaking, and splits layered-for-prereq vs force-directed-for-related, tagged ESTIMATE-to-source-verify
revisit_triggers: a prereq cycle appears in the data

nodes.definition: Preserve the user's mental map across zoom, expansion and data updates: node positions must stay stable so a user does not lose track when the view changes. Techniques are incremental layout (seed a new layout from the previous positions rather than from scratch), pinned anchors (fix meta-node/heading positions so their members expand around a known point), and deterministic seeding to defeat force-directed non-determinism [ESTIMATE — dynamic-graph mental-map preservation, to source-verify]. Stability trades against layout optimality: the mathematically best re-layout after every change would move everything, so the view accepts a slightly worse but stable layout. This is what lets expand/collapse and zoom feel like the same map gaining detail rather than a new picture each time.

nodes.definition: Place labels without overlap: node label placement is the classic point-feature label-placement problem, which is NP-hard, so it is solved with a greedy priority heuristic — order nodes by importance, try candidate label positions around each, and place a label only if it clears already-placed labels and passes the current zoom threshold [ESTIMATE — NP-hard label placement and greedy/heuristic solvers, to source-verify]. Below a zoom level only high-importance nodes are labelled at all; as the user zooms in, the element budget grows and more labels appear. Decluttering combines with SELECTION_ELIMINATION (only surviving nodes compete for labels) so the two never fight, and it is what keeps text readable instead of an overlapping smear.

nodes.definition: Choose the render target by scale. SVG draws each node/edge/label as a DOM element: crisp text, easy hit-testing and CSS styling, but the DOM bogs down past roughly a few thousand elements. Canvas (or WebGL) draws to a bitmap: it scales to far more elements but loses DOM convenience, so labels and interaction must be handled manually [ESTIMATE — standard SVG-vs-canvas rendering trade, to source-verify]. The rule: use SVG at coarse LOD levels and small graphs where crisp labels matter most, and switch to canvas/WebGL above a node-count threshold or at fine zoom over dense regions. Because the app ships no graph renderer today, this choice is open and should be made against the actual element counts the ZOOM_LOD_MAPPING and viewport culling produce, not guessed [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.5 — no graph library installed].

nodes.definition: Decide how the drawn view is actually built, given the app installs no graph library today [FACT-source: APP_RECON §5.5]. The choice is build-custom versus adopt a proven library. workflow.description: Merge semantic zoom, LOD generalization, hybrid stable layout, bundling, honest decluttered labels, transitions and culled rendering into a go/no-go
workflow.gate: the go stack, the no-go on geometric-only zoom/dishonest abstraction/invented library claims, and the legible-honest-stable acceptance rule are stated

priority_rationale: The view frame and the geometric-vs-semantic zoom distinction come first because they decide that the whole view is a semantic-zoom map, not a scalable picture; the LOD hierarchy, generalization operators, importance-ranked selection, meta-node aggregation, per-level labels and honest-abstraction rules come next as the cartographic layer that decides what is shown, hidden, merged and renamed at each level; the force-directed and layered layouts, their Barnes-Hut scaling, mental-map stability, edge bundling and label decluttering then supply the graph-drawing layer that decides where everything goes and how it stays legible; and the concrete LOD-to-render mapping, viewport culling, render-target and build-vs-adopt decisions, transitions and the final drawn-view verdict come last because they compose every upstream choice into a legible, honest, stable, scalable rendering with an explicit no-go on geometric-only zoom, dishonest abstraction and fabricated library claims.

dominance_rules.rule: Semantic zoom dominates geometric-only zoom for the concept map
dominance_rules.rationale: the few-headings-out / concise-names-in requirement needs objects to appear and rename, which geometric scaling cannot do
dominance_rules.trigger: a zoom behavior is being implemented
dominance_rules.action: implement per-level semantic zoom and never ship scale-only zoom as if it were semantic

dominance_rules.rule: Honest abstraction dominates aggressive simplification when they conflict
dominance_rules.rationale: a cleaner overview is worthless if it implies structure, completeness or mastery the data does not support
dominance_rules.trigger: a simplification would hide members or show a cosmetic roll-up
dominance_rules.action: keep member-only groupings, show counts/coverage, and use real aggregates even at some cost to cleanliness

dominance_rules.rule: Blended importance dominates degree-only when selecting survivors
dominance_rules.rationale: a low-degree but high-yield or weak concept is exactly what the learner needs to see
dominance_rules.trigger: nodes are ranked for coarse-zoom survival
dominance_rules.action: rank by a blend of centrality, high-yield and mastery relevance, not degree alone

dominance_rules.rule: Layout stability dominates re-optimizing on every change
dominance_rules.rationale: moving everything for a marginally better layout destroys the user's mental map
dominance_rules.trigger: the graph changes or the user zooms
dominance_rules.action: seed incrementally from previous positions and reset from scratch only on explicit request

dominance_rules.rule: Aggregation and bundling dominate rendering every node and edge at overview
dominance_rules.rationale: an un-generalized overview is an unreadable hairball that violates the LOD budget
dominance_rules.action: aggregate clusters into headings and bundle edges to meet the level's budget

dominance_rules.rule: Viewport culling with Barnes-Hut dominates eager full render at scale
dominance_rules.rationale: naive full layout and render freeze the browser at the app's 2000+ node scale
dominance_rules.trigger: the active graph exceeds the interactive element budget
dominance_rules.action: cull to the viewport, page within the 500-row caps, and approximate repulsion with Barnes-Hut

dominance_rules.rule: Layered layout dominates force-directed for the directed prerequisite substructure
dominance_rules.rationale: prerequisite flow must read directionally, which force-directed layout cannot show
dominance_rules.action: use layered layout for prereq edges and force-directed only for related edges

dominance_rules.rule: Canvas dominates SVG above the node-count threshold
dominance_rules.rationale: the SVG DOM bogs past a few thousand elements while canvas/WebGL scales further
dominance_rules.trigger: a level's culled element count exceeds the SVG threshold
dominance_rules.action: render that level on canvas/WebGL and reimplement label placement manually there

dominance_rules.rule: A prototyped, measured library choice dominates an asserted one
dominance_rules.rationale: specific graph libraries and their performance are unknown here and must not be fabricated
dominance_rules.trigger: a library or performance number is about to be committed
dominance_rules.action: prototype the LOD mapping against candidates and measure at the app's node counts before choosing

anti_rework_rules.rule: Fix the LOD levels and per-level element budgets before building any renderer
anti_rework_rules.prevents: authoring render code against ad-hoc levels and reworking every level when a budget is added later

anti_rework_rules.rule: Define the importance ranking before selection so survivors are consistent across zoom
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a survivor set that changes unpredictably and forces re-tuning of every level's contents

anti_rework_rules.rule: Choose the SVG-vs-canvas render target before building components
anti_rework_rules.prevents: rebuilding interaction and label placement after a late switch to canvas

anti_rework_rules.rule: Make the layout stable and incremental from the outset
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a jarring from-scratch relayout habit that has to be retrofitted for mental-map preservation

anti_rework_rules.rule: Break prerequisite cycles for layout before running the layered algorithm
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a broken layer assignment discovered only when real cyclic data arrives

anti_rework_rules.rule: Define the meta-node membership mapping before wiring labels and roll-ups
anti_rework_rules.prevents: heading contents and their labels/aggregates drifting apart and being reconciled later

anti_rework_rules.rule: Set the label collision and zoom-threshold policy before adding labels
anti_rework_rules.prevents: an overlapping label smear that must be untangled after the fact

anti_rework_rules.rule: Decide build-vs-adopt by prototyping before implementing the layout math
anti_rework_rules.prevents: hand-rolling a layout engine a library would have supplied, or vice versa

iteration_protocol.trigger: a level's culled element count grows past the SVG DOM threshold
iteration_protocol.action: switch that level to a canvas/WebGL render target and re-verify label placement

iteration_protocol.trigger: users lose track of nodes across a zoom or expand/collapse
iteration_protocol.action: tighten layout stability and tune the transition animation for object constancy

iteration_protocol.trigger: an overview level still reads as a hairball
iteration_protocol.action: increase aggregation and tighten selection to meet the level's budget

iteration_protocol.trigger: labels overlap or flicker at a zoom level
iteration_protocol.action: tighten the collision thresholds and zoom-threshold gating in the placement heuristic

iteration_protocol.trigger: force-directed layout fails to converge or oscillates
iteration_protocol.action: cap iterations, add cooling, or switch to stress majorization

iteration_protocol.trigger: a graph library is prototyped and benchmarked at the app's node counts
iteration_protocol.action: resolve the build-vs-adopt decision and, if adopted, re-verify the LOD mapping over its zoom model

iteration_protocol.trigger: a large graph hits the 500-row query cap
iteration_protocol.action: add clustered/paged loading and surface truncation honestly

required_checks: all edge ids unique EDGE_XXX format
all from/to in edges reference valid node ids
all competency_question_refs resolve to valid CQ ids
all evidence_refs resolve to valid source_registry ids
all priority_order entries are valid node ids with no duplicates
high_risk_nodes (risk_if_wrong>=0.80) have non-empty acceptance_tests and human_review_required=true
conflict edges have signed_tension<0 and resolution_rule present
observed_impact=0.0 for all nodes (no observed data)
19-24 nodes, 32-40 edges, 8-10 conflict_axes, 10-12 edge_cases, 9-12 workflow steps
post_formula_checks: all derived fields non-zero after compute run

validation_report.notes: built by kb_forge.py; run validators/kb_validator.py --mode dense to certify

test_cases.input_summary: smallest meaningful instance in this domain

evaluation_suite.regression_policy: re-run evaluation suite after any node addition or formula change
